pages.text: Ask most people what they think of snakes and the answer is the same: fear. Snakes appear in nightmares, in myths, in warnings from adults. They are associated with danger, with venom, with sudden death. This reputation is not entirely without basis. But it is enormously exaggerated. Most snakes are harmless. All snakes are fascinating. And snakes play a vital role in the ecosystems they inhabit.

image.note: Illustration: six different Nigerian snakes arranged in a grid showing diversity of size and pattern

pages.text: There are approximately 3,700 species of snake in the world. Nigeria is home to more than 130 of them. They range from tiny thread snakes barely thicker than a pencil to the African rock python, one of the largest snakes in the world, which can exceed five metres in length and weigh more than 90 kilograms.

Snakes are reptiles: cold-blooded vertebrates covered in scales. They have no limbs. They have no eyelids. They cannot hear sounds through ears the way mammals do; instead, they detect vibrations through their jaw bones. They smell with their tongues, flicking them out to collect chemical particles from the air and transferring them to a sensory organ on the roof of the mouth.

Snakes carry more myths than almost any animal. They do not hypnotise prey. They do not chase people for revenge. They are not slimy: their scales are dry and smooth, like polished leather. They do not drink milk, whatever market stories claim. A snake's only interests are food, warmth, water, and escape. Nearly every dangerous encounter begins with a snake that was trying to leave and a person who did not let it.

Because snakes are cold-blooded, they cannot generate their own body heat. They depend on the environment to regulate their temperature: basking in sun to warm up, moving to shade to cool down. In Nigeria's tropical climate, snakes can be active year-round. In cooler climates, snakes must hibernate during cold months when there is not enough heat to maintain the body temperature needed for activity.

Snakes move in several different ways. The most familiar is lateral undulation, the sideways wave that propels a snake forward across the ground. Some snakes use concertina movement, gripping the ground with one section of the body while pulling the rest forward. Heavy-bodied snakes like pythons often use rectilinear movement, a slow, straight-line crawl powered by the movement of their belly scales.

pages.text: All snakes are carnivores. They eat other animals: insects, frogs, lizards, birds, eggs, rodents, and in the case of large pythons, antelopes and even crocodiles. A snake swallows its prey whole, often head first. The lower jaw can separate from the upper jaw, allowing the snake to open its mouth wide enough to swallow prey much larger than its head appears capable of accommodating.

Most snakes kill their prey in one of two ways: by constriction or by venom. Constrictors, such as pythons, wrap their bodies around the prey and tighten with each breath, until the prey can no longer breathe. Venomous snakes inject toxic fluid through specialised teeth called fangs. The venom of different species is adapted to affect prey in different ways: some attack the nervous system, others destroy blood cells.

A snake grows throughout its life, but its skin does not grow with it. Several times a year, the snake sheds. The old skin loosens, the eyes cloud over briefly, and the snake crawls out of its own outer layer, often in one ghostly piece, leaving it turned inside out like a sock. A shed skin found in the grass is a record: from it, an expert can often tell the species and the size of the owner.

Snakes begin life in two different ways. Most lay eggs with leathery shells, hidden in warm rotting vegetation, termite mounds, or burrows, and the young cut their way out with a temporary egg tooth. Others, including many vipers, give birth to live young. Either way, parental care ends almost immediately. A newly hatched cobra, small enough to sit in a spoon, is already venomous and already entirely on its own.

The African rock python is Nigeria's largest snake. It is a constrictor, killing prey by squeezing. It lives near water and is a powerful swimmer. Rock pythons are known to prey on monitor lizards, small antelopes, and occasionally the young of larger animals. They are not venomous. They are, however, strong enough to be dangerous to humans who handle them carelessly.

pages.text: The Gaboon viper is one of the world's most venomous snakes and one of its most beautiful. Its pattern of brown, cream, and purple scales creates extraordinary camouflage against the leaf litter of the forest floor. It has the longest fangs of any snake, up to five centimetres, and delivers venom in large quantities. Despite this, it is a slow-moving snake and rarely aggressive unless stepped on, which is the most common cause of bites.

The black-necked spitting cobra is one of Nigeria's most commonly encountered venomous snakes. It can accurately spit venom at the eyes of a threat from up to two metres away, causing intense pain and, if untreated, permanent blindness. Despite this capability, the spitting cobra would rather escape than confront. Most bites and most spitting incidents occur when a person comes too close without the snake having a clear escape route.

The green mamba lives in trees in the forests of southern Nigeria. Slender, brilliantly green, and extremely fast, it is among the most difficult snakes to spot in its natural habitat. Its venom is fast-acting and potentially fatal without treatment. The green mamba is rarely encountered because it spends most of its life in the canopy, far above human paths.

The puff adder deserves its own warning. Thick-bodied, superbly camouflaged, and widespread across Nigeria, it is responsible for more serious snakebites in Africa than any other species, largely because it relies on stillness rather than escape. Where other snakes flee approaching footsteps, the puff adder freezes, invisible against the soil, until it is stepped on. In areas where they occur, the safest habits are simple: wear shoes, carry a torch at night, and watch the path.

Snakebite is a serious public health issue in Nigeria. Thousands of people are bitten each year, and a significant number die or suffer permanent injury. The greatest risk is in rural areas where people farm by hand, walk through undergrowth, and sleep on the ground. Most bites happen to feet and lower legs.

The most effective response to snakebite is antivenom, a medicine made from antibodies that neutralise the venom. Antivenom must be matched to the species that caused the bite. In rural Nigeria, access to the correct antivenom, and to the medical facilities needed to administer it, is often limited. Traditional remedies are widely used but have no proven effectiveness against venom.

Snakes are, however, extremely valuable. They control rodent populations that would otherwise destroy stored grain and spread disease. A single snake may consume dozens of rodents in a year. Removing snakes from an ecosystem causes rodent populations to explode. This is why indiscriminate killing of snakes, even venomous ones, is counterproductive.

pages.text: Learning to identify the snakes of your region, to understand their habits, and to know what to do when you encounter one is one of the most practical things a person can learn. Most encounters with snakes end safely, for the person and for the snake, when the person remains calm, does not attempt to handle or kill the snake, and simply moves away.

If a snakebite happens, the right actions save lives. Keep the person calm and still, because panic and movement speed the venom's spread. Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing near the bite before swelling begins. Immobilise the bitten limb as you would a fracture, and get to a hospital as fast as possible. Note the snake's appearance if it can be done safely, but never waste time hunting or killing it.

Just as important is what not to do. Do not cut the wound. Do not attempt to suck out venom. Do not tie a tight tourniquet, which can cost a limb. Do not apply engine oil, chalk, herbs, or a black stone, and do not wait at home to see whether symptoms develop. Every one of these traditional responses has cost lives. The only proven treatment for serious envenomation is antivenom, administered in a medical facility.

Nigeria is fighting back against snakebite. A dedicated treatment and research centre at Kaltungo in Gombe State treats thousands of patients a year and trains health workers from across the country. Nigerian scientists are working on antivenoms produced for Nigerian species, rather than imported products designed for snakes from other regions. Snakebite is now recognised by the World Health Organization as a neglected tropical disease, which is slowly bringing the attention, and the funding, it always deserved.
